chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Mechanics of Sovereign Debt Sustainability

lessons.title: The Debt Dynamics Equation: How r, g, and the Primary Balance Decide a Country's Fate

body.text: Debt sustainability is not a debt-to-GDP threshold you cross. It is a race between how fast a government's debt grows and how fast its economy grows, and the government fully controls only one side of that race.

children.text: Every year, some analyst flags a country as unsustainable because its debt-to-GDP ratio has crossed 90%, or 100%, or whatever round number sounds alarming that week. Japan has run past 260% for two decades without a default. Argentina defaulted in 2020 at under 60%. Sri Lanka defaulted in 2022 close to 100%, but plenty of countries have carried similar ratios for years without trouble. If a single debt level decided sustainability, none of this would make sense. It makes sense once you look at the actual equation governing how a debt ratio moves over time: the relationship between the interest rate a government pays, the rate at which its economy grows, and the primary balance it runs. This lesson builds that equation from first principles, so that by the end of it, a debt-to-GDP number on its own tells you almost nothing, and you know exactly what else you need before saying anything useful about it.

markDefs.definition: Changes in the debt-to-GDP ratio that come from below-the-line items, such as exchange-rate valuation effects on foreign-currency debt, bank recapitalisations, or one-off asset sales, rather than from the current year's primary balance.

children.text: A government's debt stock at the end of a year equals what it owed a year earlier, plus the interest charged on that stock, minus whatever surplus it ran on everything except interest payments, its primary balance. Expressed as a ratio to GDP, that arithmetic collapses into one identity that every debt sustainability analysis in this course, and every DSA the IMF has ever published, is built on. This version leaves out
, valuation effects and one-off items that also move the debt stock without running through the deficit; Chapter 3 brings those back in for India specifically.

body.caption: d = debt-to-GDP ratio, r = effective nominal interest rate on the debt stock, g = nominal GDP growth rate, pb = primary balance as % of GDP (positive = surplus)

cells: Debt-to-GDP ratio at the start of the year
IMF World Economic Outlook; RBI and CGA data for India
Effective interest rate paid on the existing stock of debt, not the latest bond auction yield
Union Budget: interest payments divided by average debt stock
Nominal GDP growth: real growth plus inflation, not real GDP growth alone
Primary balance: revenue minus non-interest expenditure, as % of GDP (positive = surplus)

body.text: The single most common mistake in sovereign debt commentary is plugging in real GDP growth where the identity needs nominal GDP growth. A country with 4% real growth and 6% inflation has 10% nominal growth, and it is that 10% which shrinks the debt ratio, not the 4%. Confusing the two makes stable debt paths look unsustainable and genuinely fragile ones look fine.

children.text: Why r Minus g Is the Only Number That Matters

Rearrange the identity slightly and the picture sharpens. When the effective interest rate sits below nominal growth, r less than g, the existing debt stock shrinks relative to GDP on its own, before the government does anything to its primary balance. Growth is outrunning the interest bill. When r is greater than g, the opposite happens: the existing stock grows relative to GDP by itself, and the primary balance has to work harder, running an actual surplus in many cases, just to hold the ratio flat. This one comparison, r minus g, is why headline debt ratios across countries are not comparable without it.

stats.label: r < g
stats.value: Debt ratio shrinks on its own
stats.context: Favourable dynamics; primary deficits are more affordable

stats.label: r = g
stats.context: Only the primary balance moves the ratio from here

stats.label: r > g
stats.value: Debt ratio grows on its own
stats.context: The classic snowball effect; needs a primary surplus just to stabilise

stats.label: India (illustrative)
stats.context: r < g by a meaningful margin; examined fully in Chapter 3

body.label: 5-Year Gap Between the Two Paths
body.context: Same starting debt (80%), same 3% of GDP primary deficit, same 7% interest rate. Only the growth assumption differs, 10% nominal growth versus 5%, and it alone explains a 19.6 point gap in the debt ratio after five years.

body.title: Apply the Identity Yourself
body.prompt: A sovereign has a debt-to-GDP ratio of 95%, an effective interest rate of 6%, nominal GDP growth of 4%, and runs a primary deficit of 1% of GDP this year. Using d_t = d_(t-1) × (1+r)/(1+g) − pb_t, what is next year's debt-to-GDP ratio? Answer in percent, e.g. 97.8 for 97.8%.
body.explanation: d1 = 95 × (1.06/1.04) − (−1) = 95 × 1.0192 + 1 ≈ 96.83 + 1 = 97.8%. Even a modest 1% primary deficit pushes the ratio up here, because r (6%) exceeds g (4%): unfavourable r-g dynamics amplify small deficits instead of absorbing them.

children.text: Why the Effective Interest Rate Isn't the Bond Yield You See Quoted

The r in this identity is not the yield printed on this morning's 10-year G-Sec auction. It is the effective interest rate the government is actually paying across its entire stock of outstanding debt, most of which was issued years ago at whatever rate prevailed then. India's average G-Sec maturity runs close to 12 years, so a move in the current 10-year yield takes a long time to filter into the effective rate on the stock. This is why debt sustainability can look stable for years even as the marginal cost of new borrowing rises, and why it can keep deteriorating for years after rates have already come down. Watch the effective rate implied by the Union Budget's interest payment numbers, not the daily G-Sec ticker, when you are assessing where r is actually heading.

body.text: Analysts who read a spike in G-Sec yields as an immediate sustainability threat are usually looking at the wrong r. The stock of debt reprices slowly. What a yield spike does threaten is the marginal cost of the next year's fresh borrowing and rollovers, a real risk, but a different and much slower-moving one than the effective rate on the whole stock repricing overnight.

children.text: The Primary Balance: The Only Lever a Government Fully Controls

r is set mostly by the market and, to a lesser extent, the central bank. g is set by the real economy and, again, partly by the central bank through the inflation it tolerates. Neither is something a finance ministry can dial up or down at will inside a single budget cycle. The primary balance is different: it is the direct sum of tax policy and spending decisions, which makes it the one variable in the identity a government fully controls in the short run.

body.title: Two Ways to Move the Primary Balance

columns.label: Revenue-Side Levers
points: Broadening the tax base through GST compliance and formalisation
Raising tax rates or a cess (politically costlier, slower to legislate)
Non-tax revenue: disinvestment, spectrum auctions, RBI and PSU dividends

columns.label: Expenditure-Side Levers
points: Cutting or better targeting subsidies on food, fertiliser, and fuel
Capping revenue expenditure growth below nominal GDP growth
Trimming capital expenditure only as a last resort, since that usually drags on g as well

body.title: Diligence a Finance Ministry's Claim
body.scenario: A finance ministry official tells you: "Our debt-to-GDP is only 65%, well below Italy's roughly 140%, so we have plenty of room to keep running primary deficits." You are the macro analyst diligencing this claim before recommending the sovereign's bonds to a fund.
body.prompt: What is the first follow-up question you ask, and why?
body.modelAnswer: The debt level alone tells you almost nothing without r and g. The first question is: what is this country's effective interest rate on its debt stock, and what is its nominal GDP growth rate, in other words, what is r minus g? A country at 65% debt-to-GDP with r meaningfully above g and a persistent primary deficit can be on a more dangerous trajectory than a country at 140% with r well below g and a primary balance close to stabilising. The level is a snapshot; r minus g together with the primary balance is the trajectory, and it is the trajectory that actually determines whether bondholders get repaid.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: A country has r = 3%, g = 6%, and runs a primary deficit of 1% of GDP every year. Since r sits well below g, what happens to its debt-to-GDP ratio over time, all else equal?
options: It rises steadily every year, since the government keeps running deficits
It declines gradually, since the favourable growth-interest rate gap outweighs a modest deficit
It stays exactly flat, since the interest and growth effects cancel out
It cannot be determined without knowing the current inflation rate
body.explanation: With r at 3% and g at 6%, the (r-g)/(1+g) term is worth roughly −2.8% of the prior year's debt each year, more than enough to offset a 1% of GDP primary deficit. Run the identity year by year with these numbers and the ratio declines slowly rather than exploding, even though the government never runs a primary surplus. This is exactly the dynamic that let some heavily indebted, fast-growing economies delever without ever needing painful primary surpluses.

children.text: Putting the Identity to Work: A Field Checklist

body.title: Before You Assess Any Sovereign's Debt Sustainability
steps: Find the effective interest rate on the debt stock (interest payments divided by average debt stock), not just the latest bond yield
Confirm you are using nominal GDP growth, not real GDP growth, for g
Calculate r minus g first; this tells you how much work the primary balance actually needs to do
Pull at least 3 years of primary balance data, since a single year rarely reveals the underlying trend
Check the average maturity of the debt stock; a longer maturity means r reprices more slowly after a rate shock
Only then compare the resulting debt trajectory across countries; never compare raw debt-to-GDP levels alone

body.text: The framework, figures, and country comparisons in this lesson are for educational purposes only and are not investment advice or a sovereign credit recommendation. Interest rate, growth, and primary balance figures cited are approximate and change with each data release; always verify against the latest Union Budget, RBI, and IMF World Economic Outlook data before using them professionally.

points: Debt sustainability is governed by one identity: d_t = d_(t-1) × (1+r)/(1+g) − pb_t. A debt-to-GDP level on its own cannot tell you whether a country is sustainable
r must be the effective interest rate on the whole debt stock, not the latest bond yield, and g must be nominal GDP growth, not real growth alone
When r is below g, the debt ratio shrinks on its own; when r is above g, it grows on its own and needs an active primary surplus just to hold steady
The primary balance is the only variable in the identity a government fully controls within a single budget cycle
India has historically benefited from r sitting below g, one reason its debt ratio has stayed roughly stable despite persistent primary deficits, a dynamic this course examines in full in Chapter 3
